title: The new wing's three floors and the empty fourth
summary: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh walks the new wing at Muileann chaol before its chests are carried up, and finds three floors built to hold the provinces' returns, town chronicles and vigil-books, and a fourth, raised to the same measure, left empty for a record that has not been sent.

title: Beathag's first foot-note on the empty floor
summary: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh keeps Tormod Pinn's list at the front of the year's book unchanged and adds, beneath it, her own foot-note that the fourth floor stands ready and that no cart has come, judging the sentence plainer than any she could set beside it.

title: The tally of the calling-in read floor by floor
summary: Reading the whole tally of the calling-in set out floor by floor for the first time, Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh finds that every shire the council's roll accounted for sent something, willing or not, and that the one record never asked for is the one never received.

title: The Àth leathan branch shut for falling yield
summary: The Mine Board withdraws its overseers from Àth leathan along with the branch line, its own wages no longer answering for the western pits' falling yield, and the pits pass, without any charter forbidding it, into the keeping of the hewers who work them.

title: The Àth leathan hewers pay the fifth and are entered in arrears
summary: The pit captains the Àth leathan hewers choose from their own number weigh every cart and set by the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling, sending word south each season; the Board takes the payments when a carrier brings them and enters them in its own books as arrears.

title: The first Àth leathan coal carted to Seann Bhral
summary: The pit captains at Àth leathan send the season's first coal south by cart rather than by rail, three days slower on the road but loaded and sent on the hewers' own choosing, down to the coal factors' yards at Seann Bhral in the west.

title: Sam Varley opens the pit's own book at Cnoc thais
summary: When the Board's overseer leaves Cnoc thais, Sam Varley, who has kept a private tally beside the Board's own scale for eleven years, opens a book of the pit's own accounts headed only with the day and the pit's name, the earliest page the town's register still keeps.

title: Tom Varley runs the book's errands
summary: Sam Varley's small son Tom, not yet old enough for the pit, carries the figures the book wants between the scale-house and his father's table; told that a book kept honest for nobody outlasts one kept honest only for someone watching, he carries them straight all the same.

title: An Sligeanach Fad' às sold to a family of drovers
summary: The family that kept An Sligeanach Fad' às three generations sells it to drovers new to the trade, who raise a second hall beside the first; within a few years it is the largest house on the old mining roads, grown fat on the drove trade as the coal roads empty.

title: The herring fail a second year off Seann Dunn
summary: The herring do not return, a second season together, to the grounds off Seann Dunn, and the east-coast boats, finding their own waters empty, take to fishing the grounds off Caol mhòr that the licence law has long kept for the northern boats.

title: Inis mhin's boats pass Caol mhòr's own catch
summary: Pushed from their nearer grounds by the crowding of east-coast boats, the boats of Inis mhin take the deep water beyond the northern isles; two are lost the first year and none after, and before the next season is out the catch they bring in passes what Caol mhòr itself takes from the grounds the law still calls its own.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down the keepership
summary: Mòrag nic Coinnich, two-and-seventy and thirty years and more in the chair, lays down the keepership of the Library, walking the fourth floor once more with Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh and saying only that she built the room and leaves the asking to whoever holds the chair after her.

title: Raghnall mac Mhuirich made keeper
summary: Raghnall mac Mhuirich, fifty that year, takes the chair Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down and changes nothing of the Library's hours or custom in his first year, a steadiness the clerks under him come to value in a season when little else about the kingdom's coal holds steady.

title: The fair's ceiling set on coal and broken in every stall
summary: When the Board cuts its sales and the price of coal-fuel at Muileann òg doubles, the fair's court sets a ceiling price by its long custom; within a season no factor sells at it, the coal not reaching the stalls at the named price, and the wardens do not cry the ceiling's breaking.

title: The watchmen at Cnoc fhiadhaich see nothing
summary: The Board posts watchmen of the town itself over the spoil-heaps at Cnoc fhiadhaich against households picking coal to burn; every night of the posting the watchmen see nothing, though the heaps grow lower and the poorer grates burn warmer than the fair's price could otherwise buy.

title: The capital's poorer streets burn short hours
summary: In the capital's poorer wards the street lamps burn shorter hours than the council's lighting order requires, the keepers no longer able to afford in full an order written for coal at half the price it now costs; the council's own notice calls the shortening a saving.

title: Beathag's foot-note on the capital's cold
summary: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's foot-note for the year names what the record cannot learn: how many grates in the capital's poorer wards went unlit for want of coal, a count no census asked for and no shire kept, so that the Library holds no reckoning of its own kingdom's cold.
